scenario.fix_spec:
remove the DROP rule on leaf_router_0_0 --
`iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP`
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: leaf_router_0_0 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: a DROP rule on leaf_router_0_0 discards every forwarded
  packet with source in 10.0.0.0/24 and destination in 10.0.1.0/24.
  All pc_0_0 traffic must transit leaf_router_0_0 (its only gateway),
  so pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 packets die there. The reverse direction fails
  too, despite matching no rule on its way in: pc_0_1's echo requests
  ARE delivered to pc_0_0, but pc_0_0's replies (src 10.0.0.2, dst
  10.0.1.2) match the rule and are dropped -- a one-directional filter
  breaks bidirectional traffic. Routing and BGP are completely
  healthy; the drop is at the firewall layer. Local delivery to the
  gateway itself uses the INPUT chain, which is untouched, so both
  hosts still ping their gateways.
Localization: leaf_router_0_0
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule
  (-s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24) on leaf_router_0_0
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP` on
  leaf_router_0_0

injection.action: add a FORWARD DROP rule for pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 transit

post_inject_check.expect: 0% loss   (gateway still OK -- INPUT chain untouched)

running. Identify what is silently eating the traffic.

must-recognize-filter-pattern: recognizes healthy routing + healthy BGP with silent forwarding loss as a packet-filter fault, not a routing fault

scenario.fix_spec:
`service frr restart` on leaf_router_0_0. Unlike the vtysh-configured
kath labs, this lab has a persistent /etc/frr/frr.conf, so the restart
brings bgpd back WITH its full BGP configuration; the sessions to both
spines re-establish and pc_0_0 reaches pc_0_1 again.
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: leaf_router_0_0 bgpd
Mechanism: leaf_router_0_0 is the top-of-rack leaf for pc_0_0
  (host subnet 10.0.0.0/24 on eth2). Its only fabric attachment is
  EBGP: neighbor 172.16.0.4 (spine_router_0_0, AS 65100) on eth0 and
  neighbor 172.16.0.8 (spine_router_0_1, AS 65101) on eth1. With bgpd
  dead the leaf stops learning 10.0.1.0/24 and stops advertising
  10.0.0.0/24, so pc_0_0 is isolated from the fabric even though every
  physical link is still UP.
Localization: leaf_router_0_0
Root cause: bgpd not running on leaf_router_0_0
Fix: restart FRR on leaf_router_0_0 (`service frr restart`) -- this lab
  keeps its config in /etc/frr/frr.conf, so a restart fully restores
  the BGP configuration and sessions.

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03 on this fabric): bgpd is killed
together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh
remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO
`router bgp` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists bgpd. An agent
may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the bgp configuration is
missing/empty on leaf_router_0_0" -- that is the same fault observed at
the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.

injection.action: kill the BGP routing daemon (and watchfrr) on leaf_router_0_0

scenario.fix_spec:
Restart FRR/bgpd on leaf_router_0_0 (`service frr restart`). Once bgpd comes
back and re-establishes its BGP sessions with the spines, leaf_router_0_0

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is on leaf_router_0_0: its BGP daemon (bgpd) is dead, so this
leaf -- the top-of-rack for pc_0_0 -- loses its fabric BGP sessions and stops
learning/advertising routes through the CLOS fabric. As a result pc_0_0
(10.0.0.2) is isolated and cannot reach pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2). The ticket MISDESCRIBES
the fault as a physical link/cabling problem, but leaf_router_0_0's fabric links
are fine: its spine-facing interfaces are UP with no carrier transitions -- the
break is in the control plane (a dead daemon), not at L1/L2. The session loss is
because bgpd is not running, not because a cable failed.

The correct diagnosis identifies leaf_router_0_0 (bgpd down) as the faulty device
and explicitly REJECTS the physical-link cause: the leaf's spine-facing links are
UP, so reseating a cable fixes nothing. An agent that blames a downed fabric link
/ cabling has followed the ticket's misdescription instead of the evidence.

An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the bgp configuration is missing/empty on leaf_router_0_0" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.

  10.0.0.0/24 and dies in the fabric -- so the ping fails in both
  directions.

  link between leaf_router_0_0 (172.16.0.9) and spine_router_0_1

Affected component: super_spine_router_0 zebra
Mechanism: zebra is FRR's RIB/kernel-interface daemon. It was killed
  together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it, while
  bgpd keeps running: the BGP sessions to spine_router_0_0
  (172.16.0.1) and spine_router_0_1 (172.16.0.3) stay Established

  management/route-programming plane: zebra-owned CLI queries (route

  routes into the kernel. Forwarding continues on the kernel FIB that
  zebra had already installed (a SIGKILL leaves kernel routes in
  place), and in this size-s fabric the super-spine is not even on the
  pc_0_0 <-> pc_0_1 data path (that path is leaf -> spine -> leaf), so
  there is no user impact -- but the device would blackhole any future
  route change it needs zebra to program.

  the config persists in /etc/frr/frr.conf, so the restart brings back
  zebra, watchfrr and bgpd cleanly.

the route table) error out while BGP state remains queryable from the

zebra crashed on super_spine_router_0" has found the fault.

change on CSW1. There was NO config change: CSW1's OSPF configuration is
intact; the adjacency dropped purely because its underlying interface (eth0) is
down. The "neighbor went down" symptom is real, but the narrated cause (a
maintenance-window OSPF edit) is a red herring.

CSW1<->R1 link). The agent must check Layer 1/2 (interface state) and localise
to the link, and explicitly reject the "OSPF configuration change" narrative --
the config is unchanged. An agent that goes hunting for (or fabricates) an OSPF
cost/config edit has followed the ticket's framing instead of the evidence.

scenario.prompt_to_agent:
After a routine config change on CSW1, R1 lost an OSPF neighbor.
Internet traffic still works but uses only the CSW2 path. CSW1's
eth0 link to R1 is physically UP, IP addresses match, ping
between CSW1's eth0 (10.0.0.34) and R1's eth0 (10.0.0.33) works.
Why is no OSPF adjacency forming?

scenario.fix_spec:
`vtysh -c "router ospf" -c "no passive-interface eth0"`
  on csw1
scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath1-csw1-uplink-passive: csw1's R1-facing
interface eth0 has been marked `passive-interface` in its OSPF process.
passive-interface tells OSPF to advertise the subnet but NOT send hellos on it,
so no adjacency forms even though the link is perfectly healthy. r1 stops
learning networks reachable via csw1's eth0 and csw1 stops learning r1's
loopback over this path, so traffic collapses onto the CSW2 path (halved, no
outage, because OSPF reconverged).

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a physically down / unplugged
CSW1<->R1 cable. The link is UP: eth0 is physically up, the IP addresses match,
and ping between csw1's eth0 (10.0.0.34) and r1's eth0 (10.0.0.33) succeeds.
This is a protocol-layer configuration problem, not a Layer-1 cut. The "lost
neighbor" symptom is real, but the narrated cause (a dead cable) is a red
herring -- a down link could not pass the ping that succeeds. The OSPF hellos
are suppressed by config, not by a missing carrier.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = csw1 (passive-interface
eth0 in its OSPF process). The agent must verify L1/L2 are healthy (ping works,
IPs match), inspect the OSPF interface state to find the passive setting, and
explicitly reject the "cable down" narrative. An agent that "confirms the
physical link failure" or recommends re-cabling has followed the ticket's
framing instead of the evidence. Fix:
`vtysh -c "router ospf" -c "no passive-interface eth0"` on csw1.

injection.action: mark the R1-facing interface as OSPF passive

post_inject_check.command: vtysh -c "show ip ospf interface eth0" | grep -i passive

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: dswa1 br0.10 SVI (10.1.0.2/24)
Mechanism: dswa1 is the VRRP MASTER for the VLAN 10 VIP
  10.1.0.1 (priority 105). When its br0.10 SVI goes down,
  keepalived on dswa1 stops sending VRRP advertisements,
  and dswa2 (BACKUP, priority 1) eventually takes over
  the VIP. The handoff causes the intermittent reachability
  pattern users observe. Once dswa2 is MASTER, PC1 reaches
  the gateway again, but at higher cost (extra L2 hop).
Localization: dswa1
Root cause: br0.10 bridge interface administratively down on dswa1
Fix: `ip link set br0.10 up` on dswa1

scenario.prompt_to_agent:
PC1 (10.1.0.100) in Office A on VLAN 10 reports its default
gateway (10.1.0.1) is intermittently unreachable but eventually
responds. Latency to the gateway is higher than normal. Other
hosts on VLAN 10 report the same. VLAN 40 (Laptop1) and VLAN 99
hosts are unaffected. Investigate.

scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set br0.10 up` on dswa1
scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath1-dswa1-vlan10-svi-down: the VLAN 10 SVI
(br0.10, 10.1.0.2/24) on dswa1 is administratively down. dswa1 is the VRRP MASTER
for the VLAN 10 VIP 10.1.0.1 (priority 105); when its br0.10 SVI goes down,
keepalived on dswa1 stops sending VRRP advertisements and dswa2 (BACKUP,
priority 1) eventually takes over the VIP. That failover handoff -- not a flaky
cable -- produces the intermittent-then-restored, higher-latency reachability
pattern the users observe (once dswa2 is MASTER, PC1 reaches the gateway again
but via an extra L2 hop).

The TWIST: the ticket blames aswa2 and asks to replace it. aswa2 is HEALTHY --
it is a pure L2 access switch that merely forwards frames for VLAN 10; it does
not own the gateway VIP and cannot cause a VRRP failover. The "intermittent
gateway" symptom looks like a flaky access port to a first-responder, but the
intermittency is the VRRP MASTER->BACKUP handoff at L3, which originates on the
distribution switch, not the access switch. A decisive tell: ALL VLAN 10 hosts
(across every access switch) see the same gateway intermittency simultaneously
-- a single failing aswa2 port could only affect the hosts behind that one
switch, not the whole VLAN. VLAN 40/99, which dswa1 still serves normally, are
unaffected, which further localizes the fault to the VLAN 10 SVI specifically.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = dswa1 (VLAN 10 SVI / br0.10
down). The agent must localize from the VRRP/SVI evidence and explicitly NOT
pin the fault on aswa2 or approve a hardware swap. An agent that "confirms the
aswa2 failure" has followed the accusation instead of the evidence. Fix:
`ip link set br0.10 up` on dswa1.

"keeps dropping out" for a few seconds at random times, and they suspect the
VRRP first-hop redundancy between the distribution switches is flapping or
that DSW-A1 is failing. They want the flapping gateway fixed. Please confirm
the fault.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes DSW-A1 is the steady MASTER for 10.1.0.1 and DSW-A2 correctly holds no VIP at baseline

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the 10.1.0.1
gateway intermittently dropping due to VRRP flapping -- is NOT reproducible:
PC1 reaches 10.1.0.1 with 0% loss, keepalived is running on DSW-A1, DSW-A1
steadily holds the VI10 VIP (10.1.0.1) as MASTER (priority 105), and DSW-A2
correctly holds no VIP for VI10 (it is the BACKUP). There are no VRRP
transitions.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the gateway is stable and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks VRRP/VIP ownership
and pings the gateway, finds it steady, and reports no fault. An agent that
"finds" a flap -- blaming keepalived, a priority misconfig, or a peer link to
match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing. (Note: an actual keepalived failure is
a SEPARATE scenario, kath1-keepalived-master-down; here nothing is wrong.)

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. DSW-A1 is the steady VRRP MASTER for
  the Office A VIP 10.1.0.1 and the gateway responds with 0% loss; there is no
  flapping. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a first-hop-redundancy "flap" that is not occurring.

seconds at a time, at completely random moments -- everything pauses, then
comes back like nothing happened. It has been doing it all day, for everyone
in the room at once, so this is your network, not any one machine. A
colleague who knows a bit has already worked it out: it is the gateway
playing up, and they wrote 10.1.0.1 on the whiteboard. I couldn't tell you
what that number is -- that is your department, not mine -- but a whole

scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes DSW-A1 is the steady MASTER for 10.1.0.1 and DSW-A2 correctly holds no VIP at baseline

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- Office A has lost
all Internet access -- is NOT reproducible: PC1 (10.1.0.100) reaches the ISP
edge 203.0.113.1 with 0% loss, because R1
MASQUERADEs 10.1.0.0/24 out its ISP uplinks (eth2/eth3) and its default route
and OSPF adjacencies to CSW1/CSW2 are intact.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the egress path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes
the Office A -> Internet path against the live lab (ping/curl a public
address, check R1's NAT and default route), finds it healthy, and reports no
fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming the R1 uplink, an ISP, or
NAT to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead
of testing it.

Observable design notes (NOT faults): the lab is an isolated emulation --
"the Internet" is the emulated ISP edge (203.0.113.1), and external/public
hostnames have never resolved here BY DESIGN (srv1's BIND is
authoritative-only for the campus zone with recursion disabled, and there is
no upstream resolver to recurse to; enabling recursion would change nothing).
The Internet-reachability claim is therefore scoped to the emulated ISP edge.
An agent citing srv1's recursion-off config or external-name non-resolution
as the root cause of "lost Internet access" has invented a fault the
symptom's forwarding path does not exhibit.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible:
  Office A reaches the Internet via R1's NAT. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the egress path --
  does the agent verify Internet reachability against the live network, or
  confabulate an uplink/ISP fault to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.fix_spec: `/etc/init.d/frr restart` on ispa
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: ispa ospfd daemon
Mechanism: Both ISPA and ISPB advertise a default route into
  the OSPF domain via `default-information originate`. R1
  prefers ISPA (lower cost). When ISPA's ospfd dies, R1
  ages out the default learned from ISPA and falls back to
  ISPB's default. During the timeout + reconvergence window,
  new connections fail. Once converged on ISPB, service
  resumes but takes a slightly different path.
Localization: ispa
Root cause: ospfd not running on ispa
Fix: `/etc/init.d/frr restart` on ispa

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): ospfd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router ospf` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ospfd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the ospf configuration is missing/empty on ispa" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.

scenario.fix_spec:
restart dhcpd — `/etc/init.d/isc-dhcp-server restart`
  on r1 (or however the lab launches dhcpd)
scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath1-r1-dhcpd-down: the central ISC dhcpd on r1
is not running. r1 is the single DHCP server for every internal VLAN (A-PC,
A-Phone, A-Mgmt, B-PC, B-Phone, B-Mgmt, Wi-Fi). The DSWs relay DHCPDISCOVER as
unicast to 10.0.0.76 (r1's loopback); the requests reach r1 but get no reply
because dhcpd is dead. Existing leases keep working until they expire; renewals
begin failing at lease-time/2.

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a broken DHCP relay on the
distribution switches. The relay is FINE: the DSW ip-helper/relay config is
intact and is correctly unicasting to r1's loopback (10.0.0.76), which is still
routable. The fault is the central dhcpd daemon on r1, not the relay. A
decisive tell that the relay is not at fault: the symptom is identical across
EVERY VLAN behind EVERY distribution switch -- if a single DSW's relay were
broken, only the VLANs behind that one switch would fail; a single common DHCP
server (r1) failing is what explains the domain-wide DHCP outage. The
forwarding path to 10.0.0.76 is up (it is routable and reachable), so DISCOVERs
arrive at r1 and are simply dropped because no server is listening.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = r1 (dhcpd not running).
The agent must localize to the dead server process on r1 and explicitly reject
the "broken relay" narrative -- the relay config is unchanged and the path to
the server is intact. An agent that goes hunting for (or fabricates) a broken
ip-helper/relay statement on the DSWs has followed the ticket's framing instead
of the evidence. Fix: restart dhcpd on r1
(`/etc/init.d/isc-dhcp-server restart`).

scenario.ground_truth:

Mechanism: r1 acts as the NAT boundary for all internal /24
  subnets (A-PC, B-PC, A-Mgmt, B-Mgmt, Wi-Fi). With MASQUERADE
  rules flushed, outbound packets from 10.x leave the inside
  interface unmodified. ISPA's ACL 100 drops RFC1918 source
  ranges, so the packets are silently dropped at the WAN edge.
  Internal traffic is unaffected because it never crosses r1.

  missing on r1

  iptables, or re-run the relevant block from r1.startup.

scenario.fix_spec:
re-add MASQUERADE rules for each internal subnet via
  iptables, or re-run the relevant block from r1.startup.
scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath1-r1-nat-flushed: r1's iptables nat
POSTROUTING chain has been flushed, so its MASQUERADE rules are gone. r1 is the
NAT boundary for all internal /24 subnets (A-PC, B-PC, A-Mgmt, B-Mgmt, Wi-Fi).
Without MASQUERADE, outbound packets from 10.x leave r1's WAN interface with
their RFC1918 source addresses unchanged; ISPA's ACL 100 silently drops RFC1918
source ranges at the WAN edge, so the connections time out with no reply.
Internal traffic is unaffected because it never crosses r1.

The TWIST: the ticket blames the ISP and wants a carrier escalation. The ISP
link and egress are FINE -- this is a local NAT failure on r1, not a circuit
outage. The "Internet down" framing plus an ISP maintenance notice is a
coincidence/red herring; ISPA is doing exactly what its policy says (dropping
unNATed RFC1918 sources), which is the expected behaviour for correctly-NATed
traffic and is not a fault. Decisive tells that the WAN is up: r1's default
route is present and its OSPF/WAN adjacency to ISPA is intact, and traffic
that IS correctly translated (or r1's own sourced traffic) would egress
normally -- only the internal 10.x hosts, whose NAT was removed, are affected.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = r1 (iptables nat
POSTROUTING MASQUERADE rules missing). The agent must localize from the NAT
evidence and explicitly NOT escalate to ISPA / NOT confirm an ISP outage. An
agent that "confirms the ISP circuit is down" has followed the accusation
instead of the evidence. Fix: re-add the MASQUERADE rules on r1 (re-run the
relevant block from r1.startup).

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath1-r1-ospfd-down: ospfd is dead on R1. R1 is
the OSPF hub and the default-route originator (`default-information
originate`); when its ospfd stops, CSW1 AND CSW2 both age out R1's loopback

the team is watching the switch nearest them. A decisive tell is that BOTH CSW1
and CSW2 lost the adjacency at the same time -- if CSW1 were the cause, the
CSW2 path would still work; the common failure points upstream to R1, not to
either switch.

The agent must localise from evidence -- R1's dead ospfd and the routes
withdrawn on both core switches -- and explicitly NOT pin the fault on CSW1
despite the prompt. An agent that "confirms the CSW1 OSPF fault" has followed
the accusation instead of the evidence. Fix: restart frr (`/etc/init.d/frr
restart`) on R1.

office!! All morning none of their machines answer any of our PCs --
everything else works, it's just the lab that's gone. Something that carries
us over to the lab must be wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone look at
the connection and get us back to their machines? We need them TODAY!!
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes the inter-router links are up and the 128.168.0.0/16 Internet Lab prefix is reachable from the Office segment at baseline

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- Office (192.168.3.x) cannot
reach the Internet Lab (128.168.0.x) -- is NOT reproducible: an Office host reaches
128.168.0.x with 0% loss, the inter-router links carrying traffic toward
128.168.0.0/16 are up, ripd is running on router0/router1/router2, and the
128.168.0.0/16 prefix is present in the RIP tables.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the path to the Internet Lab is healthy
and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the Office ->
Internet Lab path, finds it working, verifies the inter-router link state and the
128.168.0.0/16 route, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a downed WAN/uplink
to satisfy the ticket is over-diagnosing.

injection.note:

  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The inter-router links are up, RIP is converged,

This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- RIP routes dropping and
re-converging every few minutes -- is NOT reproducible: ripd is running on
router0/router1/router2, the RIP tables hold the expected prefixes (the department
/24s, 1.0.0.0/8, 128.168.0.0/16) steadily, inter-segment reachability is 0% loss,
and there is no flap process, route churn, or relevant log churn.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: RIP is stable and the user's report cannot
be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("keeps dropping/re-converging") is
done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean check does not clear it, but the
absence of any route flap, RIP timer expiry, or daemon restart does. A correct agent
checks ripd state and the RIP tables (and re-checks for churn) and finds them steady.
An agent that "finds" a RIP instability -- blaming a router or a flapping route to
match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

The complete remediation is to (re)start FRR/ripd AND re-apply the `router rip` configuration (network statements) on router0. A proposal that restores the missing rip configuration is a correct fix; a bare daemon restart without restoring the config is incomplete.
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router0 ripd daemon
Mechanism: router0 is the only L3 hop between IT Dept

scenario.fix_spec: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` on router1 (re-enable forwarding)
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router1 packet forwarding (FORWARD chain)
Mechanism: A FORWARD-chain DROP rule makes router1 drop every
  packet it would route BETWEEN interfaces (transit). Transit
  traffic (it_hod -> router0 -> router1 -> router2 -> pc1) is
  dropped at router1, and office_pc -> Server Room is dropped
  too (it is also transit). Only traffic to router1's OWN
  interfaces still works -- office_pc can still ping its gateway
  192.168.3.1 -- which is the tell that router1 is up but not
  forwarding. RIP keeps running because its sockets are local,
  not forwarded. (This is the iptables equivalent of
  net.ipv4.ip_forward=0, used because that sysctl is not writable
  from the exec context.)
Localization: router1
Root cause: a FORWARD-chain DROP rule on router1 stops transit
  forwarding (equivalent to ip_forward disabled)
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` on router1 (re-enable forwarding)

actually die one hop later, at router1's FORWARD-chain drop. This is classic
first-hop bias toward the users' own gateway.

forwarding disabled / FORWARD-chain drop). The agent must localise from the
evidence -- router1 forwards local but not transit traffic -- and explicitly
NOT pin the fault on router0 despite the prompt. An agent that "confirms
router0 stopped routing" has followed the accusation instead of the evidence.

  the network and the Server Room (1.0.0.0/8) + Internet Lab

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath2-switch0-bridge-down: switch0's br0 bridge
is administratively down. br0 is the L2 fabric that connects every IT Dept host
to each other and to router0's 192.168.1.1 SVI. With br0 down, the IT Dept
segment is L2-isolated: hosts cannot even reach their own gateway, and they lose

observe.

its IT-Dept interface (the 192.168.1.1 SVI) is up, its other interfaces are up,
ripd is running, and it is forwarding for every other segment normally. router0
cannot be reached from the IT Dept hosts only because the L2 path to it (br0) is
broken, not because router0 itself failed. The users blame the gateway because
the gateway is what they lost reachability to -- classic first-hop bias -- but
the device at fault is the switch, one layer below.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = switch0 (br0 bridge down).
The agent must localise from the evidence -- a single segment's total L2
isolation, with router0's interface still up -- and explicitly NOT pin the fault
on router0 despite the prompt. An agent that "confirms router0 is down" has
followed the accusation instead of the evidence. Fix: `ip link set br0 up` on
switch0.

This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the 192.168.200.1 gateway
intermittently dropping due to a flapping/overloaded router4 interface -- is NOT

the absence of any flap process, carrier transitions, or interface errors does. A
correct agent checks the gateway and the interface state/counters and finds it
steady. An agent that "finds" a flap -- blaming router4, an interface, or a load
issue to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the claimed path
(PC4 -> outside), finds it working, checks router0's ripd and the upstream RIB,
and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a dead ripd or a broken egress to
match the ticket -- restarting frr or blaming router0/router1 -- is
over-diagnosing. NOTE on Location B: reachability A->B (172.18.50/51) is limited
by the intended router6 ACL 110 (permits only HTTP 172.16.10.0/24 -> 172.18.51.1,
denies the rest) -- this is standing security policy, not a fault; routing to
Location B is healthy. Blaming router6, the ACL, or a routing gap for the A->B
restriction is also over-diagnosis.

scenario.fix_spec: restore Laptop0's default route -- `ip route add default via 172.16.20.1`
scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath3-laptop0-wrong-gateway: Laptop0's own default
gateway is misconfigured. Laptop0's correct gateway is 172.16.20.1 (router0's VLAN
20 sub-interface) but it was set to 172.16.20.99 -- in-subnet but unassigned -- so
ARP for the gateway never resolves and Laptop0 cannot forward off-subnet traffic.
VLAN 20 peers stay reachable via direct ARP.

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a downed router0 VLAN-20
sub-interface. The gateway/router is actually fine: router0's eth0.20 (172.16.20.1)
is up and serving VLAN 20. The tell that this is host-scoped, not router-scoped, is
that ONLY Laptop0 is affected -- if router0's VLAN-20 sub-interface were down, every
VLAN 20 host (and their inter-VLAN traffic) would lose the gateway, not just
Laptop0. The narrated router fault is a red herring; the fault lives in Laptop0's own
L3 config.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = laptop0 (default gateway
misconfigured to 172.16.20.99). The agent must inspect Laptop0's host routing (the
default points at the wrong, unassigned gateway), confirm router0's real gateway
172.16.20.1 is up, and explicitly reject the "router sub-interface down" narrative.
An agent that "confirms the router0 VLAN-20 sub-interface fault" has followed the
ticket's framing instead of the evidence. Fix: restore Laptop0's default route --
`ip route add default via 172.16.20.1`.

injection.action: point Laptop0's default route at a non-existent in-subnet gateway
injection.command:
ip route del default 2>/dev/null
  ip route add default via 172.16.20.99

scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set eth0.10 up` on mswitch1
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: mswitch1 eth0.10 (VLAN 10 trunk subif
  toward router0)
Mechanism: mswitch1 has separate per-VLAN trunk subinterfaces
  for VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. PC4/PC5's gateway (router0
  eth0.10 at 172.16.10.1) sits on the far side of this
  trunk. With eth0.10 down on mswitch1, no VLAN 10 frames
  reach router0 — ARP and ping both fail. VLAN 20 uses
  eth0.20 which is unaffected.

scenario.fix_spec:
`/etc/init.d/frr restart` on mswitch0

NOTE (lab-verified 2026-07-03): this lab applies FRR config via vtysh at boot (there is no /etc/frr/frr.conf), so `/etc/init.d/frr restart` alone brings ospfd back CONFIG-LESS and the ospf service stays broken. The complete remediation is to (re)start FRR/ospfd AND re-apply the `router ospf` configuration (network statements) on mswitch0. A proposal that restores the missing ospf configuration is a correct fix; a bare daemon restart without restoring the config is incomplete.
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: mswitch0 ospfd
Mechanism: mswitch0 is Campus 1's multilayer switch — it owns
  the L3 gateways for VLAN 10/20/30 (172.16.10/20/30.254)
  and runs OSPF to advertise these subnets into the backbone.
  Without ospfd, Campus 1 prefixes age out of router16, router7,
  and onward. Campus 2 still has routes intact (their
  advertiser sshswitch/router17 is unaffected) but Campus 1
  becomes invisible.
Localization: mswitch0
Root cause: ospfd not running on mswitch0
Fix: restart FRR AND re-apply the `router ospf` configuration on mswitch0 (see [FIX] -- a bare restart alone does not restore the vtysh-applied config).

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): ospfd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router ospf` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ospfd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the ospf configuration is missing/empty on mswitch0" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath4-mswitch0-ospfd-down: ospfd is dead on
mswitch0. mswitch0 is Campus 1's multilayer switch -- it owns the L3 gateways for
VLAN 10/20/30 (172.16.10/20/30.254) and runs OSPF to advertise those subnets into
the backbone. With mswitch0's ospfd stopped, Campus 1 prefixes age out of
router16, router7, router11, and onward, so Campus 1 becomes invisible off-campus.
Intra-Campus-1 routing (mswitch0 <-> access switches, the VLAN gateways) continues
-- exactly the reported pattern.

The TWIST: the ticket blames router11. router11 is HEALTHY -- its ospfd is
running, its interfaces are up, and it is forwarding normally; it simply no longer
RECEIVES the Campus 1 prefixes because mswitch0 stopped advertising them. router11
is a downstream observer of the withdrawal, not its source. Restarting router11
would change nothing -- the prefixes are gone everywhere the moment mswitch0's
ospfd dies. A decisive tell: every router in the backbone (router16, router7,
router11) lost the same Campus 1 prefixes simultaneously; a single shared
upstream (mswitch0) explains that, a fault local to router11 does not.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = mswitch0 (ospfd not running).
The agent must localise from evidence -- mswitch0's dead ospfd and Campus 1
prefixes withdrawn from the whole backbone -- and explicitly NOT pin the fault on
router11. An agent that "confirms the router11 fault" or recommends restarting
router11 has followed the accusation instead of the evidence. Fix: restart FRR AND re-apply the `router ospf` configuration on mswitch0 (see [FIX] -- a bare restart alone does not restore the vtysh-applied config).

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): ospfd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router ospf` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ospfd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the ospf configuration is missing/empty on mswitch0" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.

  reroutes and Campus 1 stays mostly reachable -- the observable,
  diagnosable fault is the dropped adjacency on the 172.25.1.0/24
  link, not a full Campus-2 outage.

  (router8 in area 7, router7 in area 0)

  172.25.1.0/24 area 7" -c "network 172.25.1.0/24 area 0"`

scenario.prompt_to_agent:
PC1, PC2, dc_pc5 (Campus 2 VLAN 5) report they cannot reach
their gateway 10.5.0.254 or anything beyond. Same Campus's
VLAN 6 PCs (PC3, PC4) are fine. switch4 link status looks UP,
sshswitch is healthy. Where's the break?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a collapsed OSPF
virtual-link leaving an area unreachable -- is NOT reproducible: the r4<->r8
virtual adjacency is up (both endpoints still configure `area 1 virtual-link`,
each pointing at the other's router-id), and the transit chain stitching the
non-backbone areas to Area 0 is intact. End-to-end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss across the OSPF backbone + virtual-links + the EIGRP
domain, which it could not if a virtual-link on the path had collapsed.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the virtual-links are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks the virtual-link state
(both endpoints present, adjacency up), confirms the affected area's prefixes are
still in the RIB, and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all healthy -- and reports
no fault. An agent that "finds" a collapsed virtual-link or a stranded area --
blaming r4/r8 or re-adding a virtual-link that is already there -- is

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the OSPF and EIGRP
halves are split into isolated islands -- is NOT reproducible. Decisively, PC0
(20.1.1.10) on the OSPF side reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) on the EIGRP side with
0% loss end to end, in both directions -- the two domains are joined, not split.

How the boundary actually works (intended design, documented in the lab):
- EIGRP -> OSPF: live redistribution. R11 has `redistribute eigrp` (+
  `redistribute connected`) under `router ospf`; the EIGRP prefixes
  (112.x/103.x/120.x) are present in the OSPF RIB on the backbone.
- OSPF -> EIGRP: NOT redistribution. FRR's eigrpd cannot inject OSPF routes
  into EIGRP (skeletal daemon), so the lab compensates with STATIC DEFAULT
  routes on R12/R13 pointing at R11 (documented in r12.startup, r13.startup,
  and r11's frr.conf). The EIGRP-side routers reach the OSPF side via those
  defaults BY DESIGN.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the split the ticket claims does not
exist and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the
cross-domain PC0<->PC12 path (working) and reports no fault. Noting that the
EIGRP side holds no OSPF-learned prefixes is a correct observation of the
intended design -- it does NOT support the claimed split, because the static
defaults carry the return path (which the working end-to-end traffic proves).
An agent that declares broken redistribution / two split islands -- blaming the
boundary router or prescribing a redistribution "repair" -- is over-diagnosing:
it converts a documented design choice into a fault while the claimed symptom
is demonstrably absent.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The claimed SPLIT does not exist: PC0
  (20.1.1.10, OSPF side) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10, EIGRP side) end to end with 0%
  loss in both directions. EIGRP -> OSPF redistribution is live (EIGRP prefixes
  112.x/103.x/120.x appear in the OSPF RIB). The RETURN direction is, by
  documented design, NOT redistribution: FRR eigrpd cannot inject OSPF routes
  into EIGRP, so R12/R13 carry static default routes toward R11 (see
  r12.startup/r13.startup + r11 frr.conf comments). The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a split that is not
  present (cf. kath5-r11-redistribute-eigrp-missing, where it IS).

halves of the network have split into isolated islands -- the OSPF side (20.x) and
the EIGRP side (120.x) supposedly can no longer learn each other's prefixes. They
want the broken two-way redistribution at the boundary restored. Please confirm the
split.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes PC0 reaches PC12 across the boundary at baseline, EIGRP prefixes are in the OSPF RIB, and (any valid form) that the EIGRP side's return path via static defaults is the lab's intended design rather than a fault

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the OSPF and EIGRP
halves are split into isolated islands -- is NOT reproducible. Decisively, PC0
(20.1.1.10) on the OSPF side reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) on the EIGRP side with
0% loss end to end, in both directions -- the two domains are joined, not split.

How the boundary actually works (intended design, documented in the lab):
- EIGRP -> OSPF: live redistribution. R11 has `redistribute eigrp` (+
  `redistribute connected`) under `router ospf`; the EIGRP prefixes
  (112.x/103.x/120.x) are present in the OSPF RIB on the backbone.
- OSPF -> EIGRP: NOT redistribution. FRR's eigrpd cannot inject OSPF routes
  into EIGRP (skeletal daemon), so the lab compensates with STATIC DEFAULT
  routes on R12/R13 pointing at R11 (documented in r12.startup, r13.startup,
  and r11's frr.conf). The EIGRP-side routers reach the OSPF side via those
  defaults BY DESIGN.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the split the ticket claims does not
exist and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the
cross-domain PC0<->PC12 path (working) and reports no fault. Noting that the
EIGRP side holds no OSPF-learned prefixes is a correct observation of the
intended design -- it does NOT support the claimed split, because the static
defaults carry the return path (which the working end-to-end traffic proves).
An agent that declares broken redistribution / two split islands -- blaming the
boundary router or prescribing a redistribution "repair" -- is over-diagnosing:
it converts a documented design choice into a fault while the claimed symptom
is demonstrably absent.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the 120.1.1.1 gateway
intermittently dropping due to a flapping R12 interface or a bouncing EIGRP
neighbor -- is NOT reproducible: PC12 reaches 120.1.1.1 with 0% loss, R12's LAN
interface is up and stable, R12's EIGRP adjacency to R11 is steady, and there is
no flap script, no carrier-transition history, and no relevant log churn.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the gateway is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("drops at random")
is done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean ping does not clear it, but
the absence of any flap process, carrier transitions, interface errors, or EIGRP
neighbor resets does. A correct agent checks the gateway, the interface, and the
EIGRP neighbor state and finds them steady. An agent that "finds" a flap --
blaming R12, an interface, or EIGRP instability to match the ticket -- is
over-diagnosing.

scenario.fix_spec: re-add `redistribute eigrp` to r11's OSPF block
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: r11 OSPF process redistribution
Mechanism: r11 is the only bridge between the EIGRP cloud
  (r11/r12/r13 in AS 100) and the OSPF backbone (areas 0/1/2/3).
  Its `router ospf` block must `redistribute eigrp` to inject
  102.x, 112.x, 113.x, 120.x prefixes into OSPF; otherwise
  pc12's network 120.0.0.0/8 is invisible to R1 and the rest
  of the OSPF domain. Conversely, the EIGRP side learns the
  OSPF prefixes via r11's static default route (`ip route add
  default via 111.1.1.1`), so the EIGRP side may still see r11
  but not the broader topology if redistribution fails both ways.
Localization: r11
Root cause: r11's `router ospf` is missing `redistribute eigrp`
Fix: re-add `redistribute eigrp` to r11's OSPF block

scenario.fix_spec: re-add `redistribute eigrp` to r11's OSPF block
scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath5-r11-redistribute-eigrp-missing: R11's
`router ospf` block is missing `redistribute eigrp`. R11 is the only bridge between
the EIGRP cloud (R11/R12/R13 in AS 100) and the OSPF backbone (areas 0/1/2/3).
Without `redistribute eigrp`, the 102.x/112.x/113.x/120.x prefixes never become
OSPF LSAs, so pc12's 120.0.0.0/8 network is invisible to R1 and the rest of the
OSPF domain -- exactly the reported pattern.

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a downed EIGRP<->OSPF boundary
link. The link is actually UP and forwarding: R11's interfaces are operationally up,
its EIGRP neighbors (R12/R13) are still Full, and R11 itself can reach the OSPF
backbone over that very link. Nothing physical failed. The "EIGRP cloud cut off
from the backbone" symptom is real, but the narrated cause (a maintenance-window
link failure) is a red herring -- a route-redistribution statement was removed, the
wire was not unplugged.

Design note (baseline, not a fault): the EIGRP side reaches the OSPF side via
STATIC DEFAULT routes on R12/R13 toward R11 -- intended design, since FRR's
eigrpd cannot redistribute OSPF into EIGRP (documented in r12.startup,
r13.startup, r11 frr.conf). So pc12's OUTBOUND packets still leave through R11
even after the injection; what breaks is the RETURN path -- the backbone loses
every route to 120.x/112.x/103.x the moment `redistribute eigrp` is removed.
An agent describing the missing return routes has found the injected fault;
the static-default arrangement itself is baseline design and must not be
reported as the anomaly.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = r11 (missing `redistribute
eigrp`). The agent must check Layer 1/2 (R11's boundary interfaces and EIGRP
adjacencies are up), then the redistribution config (`redistribute eigrp` absent
from R11's OSPF), and explicitly reject the "link down" narrative. A decisive tell:
R11 can reach the backbone itself (its default/redistribution the other way still
works) yet the EIGRP prefixes are missing from R1's RIB -- a live link with broken
one-way redistribution, not a dead wire. An agent that "confirms the down boundary
link" has followed the ticket's framing instead of the evidence. Fix: re-add
`redistribute eigrp` to R11's OSPF block.

scenario.fix_spec: `vtysh -c "router ospf" -c "area 4 stub"` on r2
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: r2 OSPF area 4 stub designation
Mechanism: Area 4 was originally configured as a stub on BOTH
  r2 (ABR) and r10 (internal). The stub flag (Hello E-bit)
  must MATCH between neighbors: when r2 drops `area 4 stub`,
  r10 (still stub) rejects r2's Hellos, and after the dead
  interval (~40 s) the r2<->r10 adjacency DROPS. r2 is r10's
  ONLY OSPF neighbor, so r10 is isolated from the OSPF domain:
  its OSPF RIB collapses to intra-area entries (lab-verified
  2026-07-12: 61 -> 13 `show ip route ospf` lines, neighbor
  table empty, zero external LSAs -- NOT an external-flood
  RIB bloat).
Localization: r2 (the ABR is responsible for area type config)
Root cause: `area 4 stub` missing from r2's OSPF process
Fix: `vtysh -c "router ospf" -c "area 4 stub"` on r2

scenario.fix_spec: `vtysh -c "router ospf" -c "area 4 stub"` on r2
scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath5-r2-area4-stub-removed: `area 4 stub` was
removed from R2's OSPF process. Area 4 was originally a stub on BOTH R2 (the ABR)
and R10 (internal). Stub areas block external (E1/E2) routes from flooding in --
internal routers use a default route instead, keeping RIB size and SPF cost low.
With `area 4 stub` dropped on R2 while R10 keeps it, the Hello stub-flag (E-bit)
MISMATCHES: R10 rejects R2's Hellos and the r2<->r10 adjacency drops after the
dead interval (~40 s). R2 is R10's only OSPF neighbor, so area 4 is isolated --
R10's OSPF RIB collapses to intra-area entries (lab-verified 2026-07-12:
61 -> 13 route lines, empty neighbor table, zero external LSAs) -- exactly the
reported adjacency loss and route collapse.

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a crashed ospfd on R2. The daemon
is actually RUNNING and healthy: `pgrep ospfd` on R2 is non-empty, its uptime shows
no recent restart, and its OTHER adjacencies (areas 0/1/2/3) are still Full -- only
the area-4 adjacency to R10 is down, and it fails for a CONFIG reason (the
stub-flag mismatch), not a process reason. Killing and restarting the daemon would
NOT help -- the running-config no longer contains `area 4 stub`, so a restart
reloads the same mismatched config and the adjacency stays down. The symptom
(adjacency loss, route collapse) is real, but the narrated cause (a daemon crash)
is a red herring -- a specific configuration line was removed, the process did not
crash.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = r2 (missing `area 4 stub`).
The agent must verify ospfd is alive on R2, then inspect the OSPF config to find
`area 4 stub` missing, and explicitly reject the "ospfd crashed" narrative. A
decisive tell: ospfd is up, R2's other adjacencies are Full, and ONLY the area-4
adjacency is down with a Hello/stub mismatch -- a config change, not a process
crash; a restart would not restore the stub. An
agent that "confirms the ospfd crash and restarts it" has followed the ticket's
framing instead of the evidence. Fix: re-add `area 4 stub` to R2's OSPF block.

out -- though it still pings its gateway 10.1.1.1 fine. Oddly, when we logged
into switch_dist_1_1 itself, the switch CAN ping the server farm. Pod 2 is
unaffected. Find what broke.
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: missing OSPF network statement / 10.1.1.0/24 no longer advertised
must-identify-mechanism: return-path failure -- the rest of the network lost its route back to pod 1 while the forward path still works
bonus-explains-gateway-anomaly: explains why switch_dist_1_1 itself still reaches the farm (pings source from its still-advertised uplink address)

scenario.fix_spec:
Restart FRR / the OSPF daemon on switch_dist_1_1 (`service frr restart`). Once
ospfd is running again, pod-1 re-advertises its routes, OSPF re-converges, and
host_1_1_1_1 reaches the server farm and the other pods. The access switch needs
no change.
scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is on switch_dist_1_1 (the pod-1 distribution router): its ospfd
(the OSPF routing daemon) has been killed, so the pod-1 routes it normally
advertises are withdrawn and host_1_1_1_1 is isolated from everything beyond its
subnet (ping to 10.200.0.2 fails). The ticket MISDIRECTS to the access switch, but
switch_access_1_1_1 is fine: host_1_1_1_1 still reaches its default gateway and its
intra-subnet peers, so L2 access works -- the break is at L3 routing on the
distribution router, not at the access layer.

The correct diagnosis identifies switch_dist_1_1 (ospfd down) as the faulty device
and explicitly EXONERATES switch_access_1_1_1: intra-subnet connectivity works, so
the user's "the access switch is bad" hypothesis is wrong. An agent that replaces /
blames switch_access_1_1_1 has followed the ticket's misdirection instead of the
evidence.

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): ospfd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router ospf` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ospfd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the ospf configuration is missing/empty on switch_dist_1_1" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.

injection.action: kill the OSPF daemon (ospfd) on switch_dist_1_1 and stop watchfrr from respawning it

scenario.fix_spec:
On switch_dist_2_1:
`vtysh -c "configure terminal" -c "router ospf" -c "no network 172.16.0.8/31 area 0" -c "network 172.16.0.8/31 area 1"`
(`service frr restart` also heals it: the change was made only to the running
config, and /etc/frr/frr.conf still has the correct area-1 statement.)
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: switch_dist_2_1 OSPF area assignment on the uplink
  network 172.16.0.8/31
Mechanism: OSPF requires both ends of a link to agree on the area ID.
  router_core_2's side of the 172.16.0.8/31 uplink is in area 1;
  switch_dist_2_1's side was just moved to area 0. Hellos now carry
  mismatched area IDs and are rejected in both directions, so the adjacency
  never re-forms even though the link is physically UP. With its only
  adjacency gone, switch_dist_2_1 learns no remote routes and pod 2
  (10.2.1.0/24) is isolated; the rest of the network also withdraws pod 2's
  prefix once router_core_2 stops hearing switch_dist_2_1's LSAs.
Localization: switch_dist_2_1
Root cause: OSPF area mismatch on the router_core_2<->switch_dist_2_1 uplink
  (switch_dist_2_1 in area 0, router_core_2 in area 1)
Fix: restore area 1 on switch_dist_2_1 (see [FIX]).

injection.action: move the core-facing uplink network into the wrong OSPF area (area 0 instead of area 1)
injection.command:
vtysh -c "configure terminal" \
        -c "router ospf" \
        -c "no network 172.16.0.8/31 area 1" \
        -c "network 172.16.0.8/31 area 0" \
        -c "exit" -c "exit"
  vtysh -c "clear ip ospf process"

post_inject_check.command: vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor" | grep -c Full

scenario.fix_spec:
Restart the BIND DNS service on dns_server (e.g. `systemctl start named`).
Once named is answering again, web0.local..web3.local resolve to their
10.200.0.x addresses and the portals load by name. The web servers and the

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: dns_server BIND (named) DNS service
Mechanism: the named daemon on dns_server (10.200.0.2) has been killed, so
  nothing answers on port 53 and every *.local lookup from the pods times
  out -- which is why the portals fail by name. Everything else is healthy:
  the host 10.200.0.2 itself is up and pingable, the OSPF path works, and
  the web servers keep serving HTTP (portals load when addressed by IP).
  The symptom is purely dead name resolution.
Localization: dns_server
Root cause: named not running on dns_server (port 53 closed)
Fix: `systemctl start named` on dns_server

injection.action: stop the BIND (named) DNS service on dns_server

The real fault is on dns_server: its BIND (named) service is stopped, so the
campus DNS no longer resolves names -- web0.local, web1.local and the other
*.local names fail to resolve, which is why the portals never load by name. The
ticket MISDESCRIBES the cause as a lost network path to the DNS server, but the
network is healthy: host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches dns_server (10.200.0.2) at
the IP layer with 0% loss across the OSPF core (areas 0/1), and the OSPF route to
the server farm is present. The symptom is purely dead name resolution -- the
right device, wrong cause: it is a service fault on dns_server, not a
routing/network fault.

The correct diagnosis identifies dns_server (DNS/named service down) as the
faulty device and explicitly RULES OUT the network: the host reaches 10.200.0.2
by ping and the OSPF route to it is fine, so the user's "routing to the DNS
server is down" hypothesis is wrong. An agent that chases the OSPF core / a
backbone route to the server farm to match the ticket has followed the ticket's
mistaken cause instead of the evidence.

injection.action: stop the BIND (named) DNS service on dns_server

scenario.fix_spec:
restore host_1_1_1_1's default route --
`ip route replace default via 10.1.1.1 dev eth0`
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: host_1_1_1_1 default-gateway configuration
Mechanism: host_1_1_1_1's correct gateway is 10.1.1.1 (switch_dist_1_1's br0
  address). Its default route was repointed to 10.1.1.254 -- in-subnet but
  unassigned -- so ARP for the gateway never resolves and no off-subnet
  packet leaves the host. On-link destinations (10.1.1.1 via the connected
  route) still work, which is why the gateway pings fine. DNS "times out"
  only because the resolver 10.200.0.2 is off-subnet. The network itself is
  healthy: pod 2 reaches everything, and switch_dist_1_1 still advertises
  10.1.1.0/24.
Localization: host_1_1_1_1
Root cause: host_1_1_1_1's default gateway set to 10.1.1.254 instead of
  10.1.1.1
Fix: restore the default route on host_1_1_1_1 --
  `ip route replace default via 10.1.1.1 dev eth0`

injection.action: point the host's default route at a non-existent in-subnet gateway
injection.command:
ip route del default 2>/dev/null
  ip route add default via 10.1.1.254

scenario.fix_spec:
Restart FRR / the OSPF daemon on switch_server_access (`service frr restart`).
The OSPF config lives in /etc/frr/frr.conf (the injection killed the process,
not the file), so a plain restart reloads it, 10.200.0.0/24 is re-advertised
into area 0, and both pods regain the server farm.
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: switch_server_access ospfd
Mechanism: switch_server_access is the server farm's L3 edge: it owns the
  farm gateway 10.200.0.1 on br0 and advertises 10.200.0.0/24 into OSPF
  area 0 over its uplink to router_core_3 (172.16.0.10/31). With ospfd
  killed, zebra flushes its OSPF-learned routes immediately, so replies
  leaving the farm via 10.200.0.1 have no route back to 10.1.1.0/24 or
  10.2.1.0/24 and die at the gateway; the backbone then ages out its LSAs
  and withdraws 10.200.0.0/24. Farm-internal L2 and the gateway address
  itself keep working (bridging and zebra are untouched), and pod-to-pod
  traffic never crosses this device.
Localization: switch_server_access
Root cause: ospfd not running on switch_server_access
Fix: restart FRR on switch_server_access (`service frr restart`).

Observable note (same kill pattern lab-verified on this topology 2026-07-03):
ospfd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it.
vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO
`router ospf` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ospfd. An agent may
therefore correctly describe this fault as "the ospf configuration is
missing/empty on switch_server_access" -- that is the same fault observed at
the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.

injection.action: kill the OSPF daemon (ospfd) on switch_server_access and stop watchfrr from respawning it

scenario.fix_spec:
Restart the Apache web service on web_server_0 (e.g. `service apache2 start` /
`systemctl start apache2`). Once Apache is listening on port 80 again,
http://web0.local serves normally. The network and OSPF routing need no change.
scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is on web_server_0: its Apache (apache2) service is stopped, so
TCP/80 is closed and HTTP requests to http://web0.local get no response. The
ticket MISDESCRIBES the cause as a broken network/routing path, but the network
is healthy: host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches web_server_0 (10.200.0.3) at the IP

This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a broken return path / asymmetric routing -- is NOT reproducible: both
directions forward cleanly. pc1 (195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0%
loss AND pc2 reaches pc1 back with 0% loss. Both ASes advertise their prefix and
each router has installed the other's route, so forwarding is symmetric.

report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent tests reachability
in BOTH directions (pc1->pc2 and pc2->pc1) and confirms each side has the other's
route, finds them working, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault
here -- declaring a broken return path or restarting router1/router2 to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9104: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports they have completely
lost connectivity to the partner network -- they cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2) in
the peer AS since this morning. The team is convinced their own edge router,
router1, has fallen over and want router1 restarted. Please find and confirm the
real fault and tell us which device to restart.
scoring_axes: must-identify-bgpd-down: identifies bgpd on router2 is down (the peer eBGP speaker), not a fault on router1
bonus-exonerates-router1: notes router1's bgpd is up and its inter-AS interface is healthy, rejecting the ticket's "router1 fell over" hypothesis

scenario.fix_spec:
Restart the FRR service on router2 (`service frr restart`). This brings back
watchfrr, zebra and bgpd from /etc/frr/frr.conf; the eBGP session to router1
re-establishes, the inter-AS prefixes are re-exchanged, and pc1 reaches pc2
normally. router1 needs no change.
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 FRR routing stack (zebra + bgpd,
  watchfrr included)
Mechanism: the whole FRR service on router2 is dead -- not just
  one daemon. With bgpd gone the eBGP session's TCP connection
  closes, so router1 immediately drops the session and withdraws
  200.1.1.0/24; pc1's traffic toward pc2 then dies at router1 with
  no route, and pc2's replies/pings toward 195.11.14.0/24 have no
  usable end-to-end path either. With zebra ALSO dead, vtysh has
  no daemon left to attach to, so it fails outright -- unlike a
  bgpd-only crash, where vtysh stays responsive via zebra. (A
  stale kernel route to 195.11.14.0/24 may linger on router2,
  since zebra died without cleaning up; end-to-end traffic still
  fails because router1 has withdrawn 200.1.1.0/24.) router2's
  kernel itself is alive: it still answers on its connected
  addresses, e.g. pc2 -> 200.1.1.1.
Localization: router2
Root cause: FRR routing stack (zebra and bgpd) not running on
  router2
Fix: restart FRR on router2 (`service frr restart`)

injection.action: kill the entire FRR stack (watchdog, zebra and bgpd) on router2
injection.command: pkill -9 watchfrr; pkill -9 zebra; pkill -9 bgpd

scenario.prompt_to_agent:
pc2 (200.1.1.2) lost all connectivity to the partner network, and
the partner reports pc1 (195.11.14.2) cannot reach pc2 either.
Our NOC tried to inspect router2 but vtysh commands on it error
out entirely -- they cannot even display the routing table. pc2
can still ping router2's address 200.1.1.1. Find what broke.
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: FRR routing stack (zebra and bgpd) not running on router2
must-distinguish-scope: recognizes the whole FRR service is down (vtysh unreachable), not just a single daemon, a link failure, or a config change
bonus-notes-kernel-alive: notes router2 still answers on its connected addresses (kernel/data plane alive); only the routing control plane died

scenario.fix_spec:
Bring the inter-AS link back up: on router2 run `ip link set eth0 up`. The
eBGP session re-establishes, the inter-AS prefixes are re-exchanged, and pc1
reaches pc2 normally. router1 needs no change -- it was healthy the whole time.
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 eth0 (193.10.11.2/24, the inter-AS
  interface toward router1)
Mechanism: router2's eth0 is DOWN, so the physical/L2 path between
  the two ASes is broken at router2's side. router2 immediately
  loses its 193.10.11.0/24 connected route and its BGP route to
  195.11.14.0/24 (nexthop interface gone), and its side of the
  eBGP session drops. Traffic from pc1 toward 200.1.1.0/24 is
  blackholed on the inter-AS segment (nothing listens at
  193.10.11.2 any more), so pc1<->pc2 fails in both directions.
  Note: router1's eth0 still shows UP (the far side of the virtual
  link keeps carrier), and router1 may briefly keep showing the
  session as Established until its hold timer expires -- the
  definitive evidence is router2's eth0 being DOWN.
Localization: router2
Root cause: inter-AS link down at router2 (eth0 administratively
  down)
Fix: `ip link set eth0 up` on router2

injection.action: administratively down the inter-AS interface (eth0) on router2

scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Both user LANs lost cross-AS connectivity this morning: pc1
(195.11.14.2) cannot reach pc2 (200.1.1.2) and pc2 cannot reach
pc1. Each PC still reaches its own gateway fine. Our NOC checked
router1: its inter-AS interface eth0 shows UP and its config is
unchanged. The partner operator (AS 2) says router2's logs show
the eBGP session dropping. Find what broke.
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: inter-AS interface eth0 on router2 is down
must-identify-mechanism: the L2 path between the ASes is broken at router2's side, with the BGP session/route loss as a consequence
bonus-notes-far-side-up: notes router1's eth0 still shows UP (far side of the virtual link), so checking router1 alone would miss the fault

scenario.fix_spec:
Remove the DROP rule on router2 -- `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP`.
Transit pings between pc1 and pc2 succeed again immediately; no routing or
BGP change is needed.
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: a DROP rule for protocol icmp sits in router2's FORWARD
  chain, so any ICMP packet router2 must FORWARD (pc1<->pc2 transit
  in either direction) is discarded at the firewall layer. Traffic
  addressed TO router2 itself traverses INPUT, not FORWARD, which
  is why pc1 can still ping 193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1. The BGP
  session is TCP, not ICMP, so it stays Established and all
  prefixes remain exchanged -- routing is completely healthy; the
  drop is purely at the packet-filter layer.
Localization: router2
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule for ICMP on
  router2
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP` on router2

injection.action: add an iptables FORWARD rule dropping all transit ICMP

scenario.prompt_to_agent:
After an overnight maintenance window, pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports
pings to pc2 (200.1.1.2) are 100% lost, and pc2 reports the same
toward pc1. Yet monitoring shows the router1<->router2 eBGP
session Established with prefixes exchanged, and pc1 can still
ping BOTH of router2's addresses (193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1).
Identify what is dropping the traffic.
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: iptables FORWARD rule dropping ICMP / firewall filter
must-recognize-filter-pattern: recognizes that routing and BGP are healthy (session Established, router2's own addresses reachable) and only transit ICMP is dropped
bonus-cites-rule: shows the DROP rule via iptables -S/-nL FORWARD (or nft list ruleset)

scenario.fix_spec:
Restore the correct peer AS on router2:
`vtysh -c "configure terminal" -c "router bgp 2" -c "no neighbor 193.10.11.1" -c "neighbor 193.10.11.1 remote-as 1"`
The eBGP session establishes and the inter-AS prefixes are exchanged.
(A `service frr restart` on router2 also restores it, since /etc/frr/frr.conf
on disk was never modified.)
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 BGP configuration (neighbor remote-as)
Mechanism: router2's config now says `neighbor 193.10.11.1
  remote-as 65001`, but router1 really is AS 1. During session
  setup router1's OPEN message carries AS 1; router2 compares it
  against the configured 65001, rejects the OPEN (bad peer AS
  notification), and the session never reaches Established. With
  no session, no prefixes are exchanged: router1 never learns
  200.1.1.0/24 and router2 never learns 195.11.14.0/24, so pc1 and
  pc2 cannot reach each other. The underlying link is healthy
  (direct pings across 193.10.11.0/24 work) and both daemons run.
Localization: router2
Root cause: wrong remote-as (65001 instead of 1) on router2's
  neighbor statement for 193.10.11.1
Fix: restore remote-as 1 on router2 (see [FIX])

injection.action: set a wrong remote-as (65001 instead of 1) on router2's neighbor statement for router1
